actions.approach: Started from scratch (exp/actions/ only had an empty cache dir). Module /Users/ianvarella/capstone_S25/notebooks/exp/actions/xclip.py builds a schedule that only looks backward in time: a call happens for a tracked person (tracker raw_id) once it has >=3 observations, then at most once per second. Each call builds an 8-frame tube from that person's last 1.5 s of observations (on low-fps sources the window is 8/fps s, capped at 8 s; frames are repeated if there are fewer than 8). All frames get the same square crop: the union of the person's boxes in the tube, padded 40%, resized to 224, then processor.image_processor. The vision tower + MIT run once per call on MPS. Cached per call: the video embedding plus the mean patch features (cache/<ds>.pt). Prompt logits come from those cached features (cache/<ds>_logits.npz). I checked my split forward against model(...).logits_per_video: max abs diff 0.0. Because of that, any prompt set or margin can be re-scored in seconds. Prompt bank: 12 positives and 8 negatives. Prompt sets: brief (the 5 positives / 3 negatives from the task), litter (6 littering positives / 3 negatives), wide (all 12 / all 8), brief_negs, litter_negs (6 littering positives / all 8 negatives). The method takes a softmax over the set and fires when the best positive prob minus the max negative prob >= margin, with a 5 s cooldown per person. The event's roi is the person's current box. Sweep: 5 sets x margins 0-0.7, method alone, with the littering lift (eval_xclip.py -> sweep_alone.csv). Selected variants were scored three ways: alone, as an add-on to baseline, and replacing reach_down (report.csv). I added a second, stronger control (xclip_controls.py). It fires the same number of X-CLIP calls per sequence but picks the calls at random from the same schedule, which separates X-CLIP's real skill from just adding candidates. Only the tune half was used (model_splits('s', heldout=False)). No GT inside methods. Feature extraction took ~13 min on MPS for 9,733 calls.
actions.summary:
X-CLIP zero-shot on person tubes is a real littering cue, but it is not an Avenue/loitering or smoking cue. Best variant: litter_negs, margin 0.2 (now DEFAULTS). Alone it gets littering crop recall 73.5 vs 56.8 for a random person at the same moments (lift +16.7, baseline +10.9) at 4.9 FA/min on normal video. It also beats random calls fired at the same rate (57.3 +- 2.5). The gain is largest on throwing (crop 30 -> 67) and tossing (28 -> 63), which reach_down misses.
- As a REPLACEMENT for reach_down: littering crop 55.7 -> 73.5, lift 10.9 -> 15.1, Avenue 68/56 -> 88/64, FA 5.1 -> 9.4/min. But smoking event recall falls 49 -> 28, because reach_down was catching smokers' hands.
- As an ADD-ON: littering crop 83.5, Avenue 88/64, smoking 55/20, FA 10.0/min. Lift stays about 11, since it only adds candidates at the same moments.
- The Avenue gain is NOT from X-CLIP: random calls at the same rate give 91/64 as an add-on.
- On smoking (1 fps), random calls do as well or better: crop 5.5 vs 3.5.
- Cost: ~206 ms vision+MIT + ~27 ms prompt head per call on CPU (measured with 5 threads while other jobs were running, load ~6, so it is probably a bit pessimistic). Busy Avenue/normal footage has 504-563 calls/min, about 2 CPU cores, more than YOLO26s itself.

actions.baseline_reference: Same harness and tune half (YOLO26s caches, partial(baseline, cfg=GateConfig())): littering event 77.0 / crop 55.7, random-person control 44.8, lift +10.9; Avenue 68.0 / 56.0; smoking 49.4 / 18.6; normal FA 5.09/min. actions.recommended: If anything, use litter_negs at margin 0.2-0.25 as a littering-only check on people. It is the only variant whose gain survives both controls: the random-person control (lift +16.7 alone vs +10.9 for baseline) and the rate-matched random-call control (73.5 vs 57.3 crop). Replacing reach_down gives the best skill per candidate (lift 15.1) but costs half the smoking recall. Adding it on top keeps smoking and adds about +5 littering crop over random calls, at about 2x the false alarms. Before shipping, two things are needed: (1) a held-out check, since prompt set and margin were picked on tune; (2) cutting the cost by calling it only on people a cheap pose or motion cue already flagged, or every 2-3 s, because calling it every second on everyone takes about 2 CPU cores on busy footage. Do not claim any Avenue/loitering or smoking benefit from it.
actions.what_failed: 1) The task's prompt set ('brief') is weak. 'a person throwing a bag in the air' wins top-1 on 582 of 2661 Avenue calls, and 'a person smoking a cigarette' also fires on ordinary pedestrians. Lift alone is only +4.9 at margin 0.5, and replacing reach_down cuts littering crop to 38. The 'wide' set (all 12 positives) has the same problem. 2) The Avenue gains (68 -> 88-96 event) are just a rate effect: random calls fired at the same rate give 91/64 as an add-on, so X-CLIP has no loitering/Avenue skill here. 3) Smoking (1 fps, gappy) does not work. An 8-frame tube there covers about 8 s of almost static frames, and random calls match or beat X-CLIP (crop 5.5 vs 3.5). 4) Low margins (0-0.1) look great on littering recall (crop 90-98) but give 20-150 FA/min. Clip-level littering event recall is near 91-100% for any method that fires often, because the clips are 3 s and every frame is positive. 5) I only tried union-box square crops, not per-frame tracked crops or other tube lengths, and did not try gating the calls on a cheap cue.
actions.risks:
- The prompt set and margin were chosen on the tune half and not checked on held-out. The positive-vs-negative softmax margin sits on a steep curve (margin 0.1 -> 0.3 moves FA from 20 to 1/min), so it will probably need recalibrating per camera or domain.
- The littering clips are 1080p close-ups while the normal footage is 640x360 Avenue. Part of the gap between how often it fires on littering clips and on normal video may be domain or resolution rather than action.
- The CPU latency (206 ms vision + 27 ms prompt head + ~60 ms crop/preprocess on 1080p jpgs) was measured while sibling experiments were loading the machine (load avg ~6), so it is somewhat pessimistic. Even so, about 500+ calls per minute of busy footage (about 9 tracked people) means about 2 CPU cores, more than YOLO26s itself; deploying it needs gating or a lower call rate.
- It uses raw tracker ids, not stitched ids, so a broken track restarts its 5 s cooldown.
- The cache directory is shared with sibling action experiments; the xclip files are only <ds>.pt (~0.5 GB total) and <ds>_logits.npz.

actions.approach:
I built a skeleton-sequence classifier on the YOLO26s-pose keypoints Stage 1 already caches, so YOLO is not re-run. Each tracked person (tracker raw_id) is checked at most once per second, starting after 0.8 s of track history. A check takes the last 1.0 s of that track only (causal) and resamples it to K=8 steps, using the latest observation at or before each step. Keypoints are taken relative to the hip centre and divided by the track's median box height so far. Each step also carries a visibility mask, keypoint velocities in body heights per second, hip-centre velocity, box height compared with the track's usual height (to catch crouching), box aspect and a frame-border flag. The summary feature vector (about 200 values) holds the per-keypoint mean, min, max and range, max and mean keypoint speed, wrist extension, wrist-below-knee and torso length. Absolute pixel size was removed on purpose, because it gives the camera away (littering footage is 1080p, Avenue is 360p).

Models: lr_sum (numpy L2 logistic regression), mlp_sum (torch, 1 hidden layer of 32 with dropout) and gru_seq (torch GRU with 32 hidden units on the 8-step sequence). Each has a twin ending in _lit, trained without the normal-video negatives.

Labels (used only in build()): a window is the actor (1) if the person box has IoU >= 0.4 with the GT box, a bystander (0) if IoU < 0.15, and is dropped in between. Tune normal videos add negatives. Training rows: 646 actor windows, 1441 bystander windows, 2482 normal-video windows. Cross-validation uses 5 folds, grouped by clip and stratified by action, with normal videos split by video. Every littering clip and normal video is scored by a fold model that never saw it. Avenue and smoking are scored by the model trained on everything. The threshold is set on the out-of-fold normal scores to hit a target false-alarm rate (0.5, 1, 2 or 4 per minute), with a 5 s cooldown per track. The method emits pose_action events through make_event and never reads GT. A sequence not in the cache is extracted live and scored by the full model.

Because the stock random control turned out to be gameable (see what_failed), I also built a stricter control that gives same-moment events to distinct random people, plus matched-rate references (reach_down only, a tallest-person-in-frame prior, firing once on every person), a within-clip actor-vs-bystander AUC, and a count of littering-camera candidates landing on bystanders.

Compute: about 50 s to build all 6 variants on CPU, about 30 s per full evaluation sweep and about 3 min for the diagnostics. MPS was not needed.
actions.summary:
The learned pose model works on the littering clips. At the same number of candidates per clip it picks the right person more often than reach_down does. The tune-half normal false-alarm rate is optimistic because of a camera confound.

Best variant is mlp_sum with the threshold set for 1 false alarm per minute on tune normal video. On its own it gets littering crop recall 73.5%, against 54.8% for reach_down alone. Its stock lift is +22.2 (reach_down +11.8). With the stricter distinct-person control it is +19.0 (reach_down +9.9, tallest-person prior +12.8), at about the same 1.39 candidates per clip as reach_down's 1.36. The out-of-fold within-clip actor-vs-bystander AUC is 0.747, against 0.707 for "taller box is the actor", so part of the gain is a size or closeness prior.

As an add-on to the baseline: littering 97.0% event / 87.0% crop, Avenue 84/64, smoking 56.6/22.6, normal false alarms 6.07 per minute. The baseline gives 77.0/55.7, 68/56, 49.4/18.6 and 5.09.

Replacing reach_down: littering 90.0/73.5 with lift +20.9 (fair +17.9), Avenue 84/60, false alarms 5.49 per minute. Smoking drops to 29.4/9.6, because reach_down was producing many of the smoking candidates and at 1 fps a 1 s window holds only 1-2 frames.

CPU cost is about 0.22 ms per call for features plus 0.004 ms (LR), 0.028 ms (MLP) or 0.10 ms (GRU) for the model. Calls per minute: 486 on normal Avenue video, 421 on Avenue test (raised by short tracklets restarting the per-track timer), 186 on littering clips and 33 on smoking. That is negligible next to the roughly 100 ms per frame YOLO26s costs.

Main caveat: on the littering camera the same threshold puts about 13 candidates per minute on bystanders, against 1 per minute on Avenue normal footage. reach_down shows the same jump: 16.3 per minute on littering bystanders against 0.59 on normal. So the normal-video false-alarm figures do not carry over to other cameras, and the threshold needs per-camera normal footage.

Outputs: per-variant results in /Users/ianvarella/capstone_S25/notebooks/exp/actions/pose_seq_results.csv. Cached scores and models are in /Users/ianvarella/capstone_S25/notebooks/exp/actions/cache/: scores.pkl, model_*.pkl, cv_report.json, calls.json, timing.json and diagnostics.json.

actions.baseline_reference:
Same code, YOLO26s tune half, partial(exp_harness.baseline, cfg=GateConfig()):
- Baseline: littering 77.0% event / 55.7% crop, stock lift +10.9 (control 44.8 ± 2.7); Avenue 68/56; smoking 49.4/18.6; normal false alarms 5.09 per minute.
- reach_down only: littering 73.9/54.8, lift +11.8; Avenue 28/28; smoking 43.4/15.4; 0.59 false alarms per minute.
- Baseline minus reach_down: littering 7.0/1.3; Avenue 68/52; smoking 10.7/4.2; 4.51 false alarms per minute.
- Stricter control (same-moment events go to distinct random people): baseline +10.3, reach_down +9.9, tallest-person prior +12.8 at 1.19 candidates per clip (19.6 normal false alarms per minute), fire once on every person +3.8 (its stock lift is +22.5).
- Within-clip actor-vs-bystander AUC of the trivial "taller box" score: 0.707.
- Littering-camera candidates on bystanders: reach_down 16.3 per minute, baseline 17.4.
actions.recommended:
mlp_sum, threshold set for 1 false alarm per minute on tune normal video (5 s cooldown, about one call per person per second), as an ADD-ON that keeps reach_down. Tune half: littering 97.0% event / 87.0% crop, Avenue 84/64, smoking 56.6/22.6, normal false alarms 6.07 per minute (baseline 5.09).

On its own it beats the random control by more than reach_down does at the same candidate count: stricter-control lift +19.0 vs +9.9, stock lift +22.2 vs +11.8. Do not use it as a replacement for reach_down: smoking event recall falls from 49 to 29 because the 1 s window is too short at 1 fps.

Before shipping:
1. Measure once on the held-out half.
2. Check the threshold on normal footage from each deployment camera; the Avenue-calibrated threshold does not carry over.
3. Train with 3-5 seeds to check the MLP's stability (only one seed was run).
actions.what_failed:
1. The stock random control is gameable. It samples with replacement, so firing once on every person gets lift +22.5 for free (+3.8 with the distinct-person control). Raw stock-lift numbers for high-rate variants are therefore inflated. Compare at matched candidates per clip using the stricter control in pose_seq.diagnose().

2. The _lit variants, trained only on littering clips without normal-video negatives, have the best within-clip actor-vs-bystander AUC (lr_sum_lit 0.771) but are unusable with a threshold set on normal video. They score ordinary Avenue walkers higher than littering actors, so at 1 false alarm per minute recall drops to 7-15% (stricter lift about 0). The normal negatives make calibration work largely by telling the two cameras apart, not by learning the action.

3. The learned models only modestly beat a size prior: within-clip AUC 0.73-0.75 against 0.707 for "taller box is the actor". Some of the gain is "the person closest to the camera".

4. The logistic regression is weak at low false-alarm rates (36% crop at 1 per minute). gru_seq is no better than the MLP on summary features and gives poor Avenue crops (8% alone).

5. Smoking (about 1 fps) is out of reach: a 1 s window holds 1-2 frames, so there are no usable velocities.

6. The tune normal set is small (8 videos, 5.1 min) and comes from the same Avenue camera as the Avenue test videos. The threshold was set on the same normal videos used to report false alarms (out-of-fold for the model weights, in-sample for the threshold).
actions.risks:
- Camera shift: the normal false-alarm rate is set on the Avenue camera. On the 1080p littering camera the same threshold fires about 13 times per minute on bystanders (reach_down 16 per minute there). Real false alarms depend on per-camera calibration, which needs normal footage from each camera.
- The model may partly learn camera or resolution cues (keypoint visibility, crop geometry) rather than the action. Absolute pixel size was removed, but the confound remains.
- Positives are all windows of the actor, not just the moment of the throw, so the model also learns who tends to be the actor (posture, closeness).
- Only one training seed and only the tune half; the held-out half has not been measured (it must be run once with STAGE1_HELDOUT).
- Fragmented tracklets restart the per-track timer and raise calls per minute (about 420-490 on Avenue). CPU cost stays negligible at about 0.25 ms per call.
- Other agents write to the same cache directory. My files are scores.pkl, model_{variant}.pkl, cv_report.json, calls.json, calls_summary.json, timing.json and diagnostics.json there, plus /Users/ianvarella/capstone_S25/notebooks/exp/actions/pose_seq_results.csv.
- Reproduce with ../.venv/bin/python exp/actions/pose_seq.py build | eval | timing | diagnose, run from notebooks/.

actions.approach:
I wrote /Users/ianvarella/capstone_S25/notebooks/exp/actions/videomae.py, which uses MCG-NJU/videomae-base-finetuned-kinetics with no fine-tuning. People are tracked with the same TrackStitcher ids the rule engine uses: I replay RuleEngine with rules=() on the cached YOLO26s observations. Each tracked person is checked at most once per second. At 10-12.5 fps a check needs 0.5 s of track history; on the 1 fps smoking camera a person is checked right away. The tube is the person's last 1.6 s (4 s on the 1 fps camera), using only frames <= t. From it I sample 16 frames evenly, repeating frames when there are fewer than 16. Each frame is a square crop 1.3x the largest box side, centred on that frame's box, resized to 224, RGB with ImageNet normalisation. I checked a few tubes by eye and they look right. The cue is the softmax mass on a class group: smoke {smoking, smoking hookah}; throw {catching/throwing baseball/frisbee/softball, hammer, javelin, throwing axe/ball/discus, tossing coin}; litter = throw + kick + pick (+ garbage collecting). The method fires make_event(f"action_{group}", t, person box) with a 3 s cooldown per person. It never reads ground truth.

Every scheduled call is cached once: logits (float16) plus t, cid, box and frame count, in exp/actions/cache/videomae/<dataset>.pkl. I put these in a subfolder because the parallel xclip.py and pose_seq.py agents write into exp/actions/cache/. The offline build ran on MPS in fp16 (max softmax difference from fp32 is 0.001) and took about 31 minutes for 13,574 calls. Threshold sweeps read only the cache.

The scoring is in exp/actions/eval_videomae.py: `diag` gives per-person AUROC (ground truth used only for analysis) and `sweep` writes cache/videomae/results.csv. Random-control lift uses 10 seeds. CPU latency is in exp/actions/latency_videomae.py, which writes cache/videomae/cpu_latency.json. Everything used the tune half only; held-out was never loaded.
actions.summary:
VideoMAE/Kinetics gives a modest but real throwing cue on the littering clips and no smoking cue at all.

Per-person AUROC (the ground-truth actor vs other people at the same calls):
- Throw mass on littering: 0.635 overall. By action: throwing 0.79, tossing 0.64, dropping 0.59, dumping 0.60, putting-down 0.51.
- Smoke mass on the smoking set: 0.486, which is chance. On the right person the smoking class mass has a median of 0.002, and the model's top-1 guesses on those people are "water skiing", "abseiling" and "laying bricks". At 1 fps most tubes are a single repeated still, and the cigarette is a few pixels.
- Smoke mass on Avenue: 0.26, so it fires more on non-anomalous people.

Best operating point: baseline + throw mass >= 0.10 as an add-on.
- Littering crop recall goes from 55.7 to 79.6, and event recall from 77.0 to 91.3.
- Lift over the random-person control goes from +10.9 to +17.2 (control standard deviation about 2.4).
- Per action, crop recall changes: throwing 30 to 80, tossing 28 to 63, dropping 41 to 76. Dumping (100) and putting-down (78) are unchanged, because reach_down already catches them.
- Avenue event recall goes from 68 to 76, but crop recall stays at 56. The two extra events are hit in time on the wrong person, so this is not real skill.
- Smoking goes from 49.4/18.6 to 52.7/20.3. That is incidental firing, not smoking detection.
- Normal false alarms go from 5.09 to 5.68 per minute.

The cue alone (throw >= 0.10) gives 0.59 FA/min with lift +11.6. It is complementary to reach_down, not a substitute.

Cost is the main problem: 577 ms per call on CPU, plus about 34 ms to build the tube. On busy footage (Avenue/normal) that is about 440-490 calls per minute, or roughly 4.5 CPU-minutes of compute per minute of video.

actions.baseline_reference:
All runs use the same code: tune half, YOLO26s caches, partial(exp_harness.baseline, cfg=GateConfig()), exp_harness.score, and random_control.lift with 10 seeds.
- Baseline: littering event 77.0 / crop 55.7, random control 44.8 +- 2.7, lift +10.9. Avenue 68.0/56.0 (51.6% of video skipped). Smoking 49.4/18.6. Normal false alarms 5.09 per minute.
- Baseline minus reach_down: littering 7.0/1.3 (lift -1.3), Avenue 68/52, smoking 10.7/4.2, FA 4.51.
- Baseline per-action crop recall: dropping 41.3, dumping 100, putting-down 78.3, throwing 30.4, tossing 28.3.
- VideoMAE call volume (tune half): littering 2,226 calls (194 per min), Avenue 2,317 (439 per min), normal 2,513 (492 per min), smoking 6,518 (71 per min).
- CPU latency: 577 ms median, 645 ms p90 per call (batch 1, 16x224x224, 5 torch threads, measured while other jobs were running), plus 34 ms to build the tube from 1080p frames. MPS fp16 offline: about 105 ms per call.
actions.recommended:
As an experiment, use only the throw group (throw mass >= 0.10) as an ADD-ON next to reach_down, not as a replacement. On the tune half that gives:
- Littering crop recall 55.7 -> 79.6, and lift over random +10.9 -> +17.2.
- Throwing, tossing and dropping all improve sharply.
- About +0.6 false alarms per minute on normal video.
- throw >= 0.20 is a zero-extra-false-alarm alternative: crop 65.2, lift +14.3.

Do not use the smoke group, and do not use the broad litter group at 0.05-0.10.

Before integrating:
- Measure once on the held-out half.
- Fix the cost. At about 470 calls per minute times 0.58 s on busy footage, it does not run in real time on CPU. It needs a cheap pre-gate, such as only checking people whose wrist or arm speed is high or who are not already flagged, or a cap on concurrent people. Without a gate it should stay an offline or second-stage check on a few people.
actions.what_failed:
- **Smoking: complete failure.** Per-person AUROC is 0.486 on the smoking set. The smoking classes get median mass 0.002 on the right person and never cross 0.05 there. The model's top-1 guesses on smokers are water skiing, abseiling and laying bricks. Causes: at 1 fps with fragmented tracks most tubes are one still frame repeated 16 times, and the cigarette is tiny at 640x480 CCTV. Meanwhile the smoke cue fires on ordinary Avenue/normal people: AUROC 0.26 on Avenue, and FA rises from 5.1 to 11.2 per minute at threshold 0.05. Every smoking-set gain in the tables comes from throw/litter firing on random people, not from smoking detection.
- **As a reach_down replacement it loses recall.** Littering crop falls to 43 (vs 55.7) because dumping and putting-down collapse to 15-17. Kinetics has nothing like "set an object down"; per-action AUROC for putting-down is 0.51.
- **Broad class groups (litter mass) are not a skill signal.** At 0.05-0.10 they raise recall mostly by firing on many people (17-64 FA per minute when used alone).
- **Avenue gain is not real.** Avenue event recall rises 68 -> 76 with throw >= 0.10, but the crop recall does not change: the 2 newly covered events are hit in time on the wrong person.
- **Pick and kick classes carry nearly no information** (pick AUROC 0.51 on littering).
- **Not tested:** a cross-validated linear probe on the 400 logits; a cheaper motion-gated schedule; a smaller or distilled model.
actions.risks:
- **Domain dependence.** The throw cue fires far more on the close, high-resolution littering clips (201 events in 11.5 minutes) than on Avenue (15 in 5.3 minutes) or normal video (3 in 5.1 minutes). The low false-alarm rate may partly reflect small, distant people in Avenue rather than specificity, so a closer camera could produce many more false alarms.
- **Thresholds were chosen on the tune half** (0.10/0.20 from a sweep of 4 values). Held-out has not been run.
- **Possible motion confound.** The throw signal may partly be "this person is moving their arms". A simple wrist-speed cue was not compared, so the gain may not need a 86M-parameter model.
- **Small, all-positive clips.** The littering clips are 3 s and all-positive. The +6.3 lift gain over baseline is about 2.5 standard deviations of the random control, and it comes from 230 clips.
- **Compute.** 577 ms per call on CPU at about 470 calls per minute is roughly 4.5x real time on 5 threads. MPS fp16 was used only offline.
- **Shared cache folder.** The parallel xclip.py and pose_seq.py agents write into exp/actions/cache/ and also wrote into my build.log. My caches are in exp/actions/cache/videomae/, which the module now points to.
- **No other files modified.** I created only videomae.py, eval_videomae.py and latency_videomae.py under exp/actions/.
